scenes.heading: Dockerizing & Deploying Go Services
scenes.narration: Let's see why Go is the best-behaved citizen in a container, and how to package and deploy a Go service the right way.

scenes.heading: Why Go loves containers
items: go build produces one static binary, no runtime to ship
Multi-stage builds compile fat, then ship tiny
Scratch or distroless images measured in single-digit megabytes
scenes.narration: Go is uniquely suited to containers because go build produces a single static binary with no interpreter or shared libraries to ship. The whole packaging story rests on one pattern: the multi-stage Dockerfile. A fat builder image compiles the binary, then a tiny final stage on scratch or distroless ships just that binary, giving you images measured in single-digit megabytes instead of hundreds.

scenes.heading: The multi-stage build pipeline
steps: Copy go.mod/go.sum, run go mod download (cached layer)
Copy source, build a CGO_ENABLED=0 static binary
COPY only the binary across from the build stage
Run as non-root; wire Kubernetes probes
scenes.narration: The pipeline layers for cache hits: copy the module files and run go mod download first, so dependencies stay cached across code edits. Then copy the source and compile a static binary with cgo disabled. A second FROM starts a minimal distroless stage, and you copy only the finished binary across, discarding the compiler and source. Finally you run as a non-root user and wire up Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes.

scenes.heading: Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM
scenes.narration: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM before killing a pod, so a Go service must catch it and drain instead of exiting abruptly. Using signal.NotifyContext you get a context cancelled on SIGTERM; you run the server in a goroutine, block on context done, then call server Shutdown with a deadline a bit under the pod's grace period. That stops accepting new connections and lets active handlers finish, which is exactly what makes rolling deploys zero-downtime.

scenes.text: Without CGO_ENABLED=0 the binary dynamically links libc and crashes on scratch with 'no such file or directory'.
scenes.narration: The most common trap: the default go build may dynamically link libc through cgo, and a scratch image has no libc or dynamic loader, so the binary crashes with a confusing 'no such file or directory'. Building with CGO_ENABLED=0 forces the pure-Go implementations and produces a fully static binary that actually runs on an empty base image.

scenes.text: Multi-stage + static + distroless + SIGTERM draining = tiny, secure images that deploy with zero downtime.
scenes.narration: Put it together: a multi-stage Dockerfile with a static binary on distroless turns a nine-hundred-megabyte image into about ten, run as non-root for a small attack surface, config passed via environment variables, and SIGTERM draining for zero-downtime deploys. That's the standard shape for shipping Go to Kubernetes.
